analysis.one_liner: Sets federal design-safety rules for handguns and new duties on dealers and gun owners to keep guns away from children.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote; it died in the Senate Judiciary Committee when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have banned manufacture of handguns that fail drop tests, lack child-resistant triggers, or can fire without their magazine; extended the ban on selling handguns to minors to assault weapons; revoked dealers' licenses for willfully selling to minors; required two IDs from buyers under 24; set safety standards for gun shops; made adults criminally liable if a child gets an unsecured loaded gun and someone is hurt; and funded CDC injury tracking, school gun-violence education, and gun tracing. It was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Families and communities would benefit from handguns designed not to fire when dropped or handled by a young child, from tighter dealer accountability, and from criminal liability for leaving loaded guns accessible to children [S2][S3]. Schools and local health departments would receive federal grants for gun-violence education and injury surveillance [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Bans manufacture or import of 'unsafe handguns' — those that fire when dropped, lack a child-resistant trigger, fire without a magazine, or lack an unauthorized-user locking device — with an 18-month compliance window [S2][S3].

Automatically revokes a dealer's federal license for willfully selling a gun to a minor, requires two photo IDs from buyers believed under 24, and sets minimum safety and security standards for gun shops with annual ATF inspections [S2][S3].

Makes it a federal crime, punishable by up to a year in prison or a $10,000 fine, to leave a loaded gun accessible to a child who then causes injury — with exceptions for locked storage, self-defense, and law enforcement [S2][S3].
Extends the existing juvenile handgun ban to semiautomatic assault weapons and doubles the penalty for arming a juvenile for a violent crime [S2][S3].

Authorizes $5 million a year through 2003 for CDC-administered state tracking of child firearm injuries, $60 million a year through 2001 for school gun-violence education grants, and grants to expand gun tracing to 250 cities by 2003 [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Gun manufacturers would bear redesign and testing costs, and gun dealers the cost of shop security upgrades, extra record-keeping, and inspection compliance [S3]. Gun owners who store loaded firearms where children can reach them would face federal penalties [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Gun makers, dealers, and some owners

drawbacks.text: The design and shop-security mandates would impose real compliance costs on manufacturers and small dealers, and the safe-storage offense could expose otherwise lawful gun owners to federal prosecution if a child gains access and someone is harmed [S3].

The bill gives the Treasury Secretary broad rule-making discretion over what counts as a child-resistant trigger or an unauthorized-user device, which critics of such mandates have argued creates uncertainty for an entire product line and amounts to a form of government design control over firearms [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-health benefit — fewer children shot accidentally or by peers, better data on child gun injuries, and traffickers tracked — is large and the compliance costs fall on a specific industry. The safe-storage offense is written with exceptions (locked storage, self-defense, no reasonable expectation a child is present) that blunt the risk to careful owners, though the mandatory design standards would depend heavily on how the Treasury wrote the rules.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never held a hearing or vote on it, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Edward Kennedy introduced the Children's Gun Violence Prevention Act of 1998 on June 17, 1998, joined by Boxer, Dodd, and Reed [S5][S3].
Ten senators, all Democrats, cosponsored the bill [S4].

The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced; the action history shows no further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — before the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Gun manufacturers and dealers avoided new design mandates, license-revocation rules, and inspections; no new federal protections for children from guns were enacted.

for.name: Sen. Edward M. Kennedy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor

against.name: Orrin Hatch
against.what_they_did: The committee he chaired never held a hearing or vote on the bill, and it died there

sides.party_line_note: All 11 sponsors were Democrats and none were Republicans; the bill never reached a vote, so there is no roll-call record of how the chamber would have split.

industries.note: They would have had to redesign or stop selling handguns that fail drop tests or lack child-resistant triggers and unauthorized-user locks, and could still face state lawsuits [S3]. Their cost is the safety benefit for families.

Automatic license revocation for willfully selling to minors, two-ID checks for younger buyers, minimum shop-security standards, and routine inspections would have raised their compliance and operating costs [S3].

industries.industry: Gun lock, safe, and safety-device makers
industries.note: The bill requires locking devices on new handguns and defines approved secure-storage devices, creating demand for their products [S3].
